report:
**Conclusion: the claim is not supported.** Available evidence does not show that taking ibuprofen worsens COVID-19 infection or outcomes.

The concern arose early in the pandemic from theoretical mechanisms and anecdotal reports, rather than convincing patient-level evidence. The World Health Organization’s review found no direct evidence at that time from COVID-19, SARS, or MERS patients and therefore judged the available evidence indirect. UK medicines regulators similarly concluded there was insufficient evidence for a link between ibuprofen (or other NSAIDs) and either contracting COVID-19 or worsening it.

Later literature reviews found no scientific evidence that ibuprofen increases ACE2 expression—the proposed mechanism for worse infection—and note that its appropriate use for fever or pain should be determined by its usual benefit–risk profile, not a presumed COVID-specific danger.

Ibuprofen still has its ordinary risks: it can cause or worsen stomach bleeding/ulcers, kidney injury, and some cardiovascular problems, and may be unsuitable for particular people or drug combinations. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period, follow the label or clinician advice, and seek prompt medical care for severe or worsening COVID-19 symptoms. It treats fever and pain; it is not an antiviral COVID-19 treatment.

Sources:  
- World Health Organization: https://www.who.int/news-room/commentaries/detail/the-use-of-non-steroidal-anti-inflammatory-drugs-(nsaids)-in-patients-with-covid-19  
- UK Commission on Human Medicines/MHRA: https://www.gov.uk/government/news/commission-on-human-medicines-advice-on-ibuprofen-and-coronavirus-covid-19  
- PubMed review: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34196258/  
- PubMed review on benefit–risk considerations: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32415494/
